title: Shortage Pilgrimage
lessons: the tin hunt was real and it was lore
scarcity did the marketing for free
capacity capex is a confession of demand

intro.speaker: ZYN
text: Aisle five. Behold: the hook where I used to live.
You already know me, so no pitch. Just the empty shelf and what it did to people.

choices.text: Summer '24. I drove to three stores for one tin.
There was a shortage? Genuinely never noticed.
Empty shelves usually mean somebody planned something.

branch-veteran.speaker: ZYN
text: A pilgrim! Go on: parking lots, phone calls ahead, one can rationed like gold.
People were paying resale for flavored gum-pillies. Incredible era.

branch-tourist.speaker: ZYN
text: Lucky you. Everyone else was doing store-to-store treasure hunts.
Scarcity looked great on nobody. Except, statistically, on me.

branch-economist.speaker: ZYN
text: ...We'll get there. Walk with me first.
You're going to make me say the quiet part in aisle five, aren't you.

hunt.speaker: ZYN
text: Early '24: shipments up eighty percent in a quarter, and the shelves still went bare.
That's when zynnies became folklore you couldn't buy. Want something? Tell it it's rare.

tension.speaker: ZYN
text: Mid-shortage we announced new plants. Six hundred million in Colorado, more in Kentucky.
Demand outran supply so hard we built factories about it. The shortage did our marketing free of charge.

choices.text: Turning 'we ran out' into a legend. Genuinely elite.
Or the desire was engineered, then billed as destiny.

wrap.speaker: ZYN

text: Three-store pilgrim, meet the supply chain that sent you on pilgrimage.
You two have technically met. This is the reunion.
See? Quiet part, aisle five. You didn't even flinch.
$832 million says you were right to squint.
Restock truck comes Thursday. The mythology restocks itself either way.
Take the last tin if you see one. Or leave it — scarcity needs witnesses.
